Welcome to STAT 312! Engineers and scientists routinely work with data that contain variability and uncertainty. For example, how can we determine whether a change in a manufacturing process actually improves product quality? How can we use measurements from a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population? How can we quantify uncertainty when comparing two designs, estimating an unknown quantity, or predicting future performance?
Statistics and probability provide a framework for answering these questions. They allow us to collect and summarize data, understand variability, quantify uncertainty, draw meaningful conclusions, and make informed decisions.
Throughout the semester, we will develop the fundamental statistical and probabilistic tools used in engineering and scientific problem solving. Topics will include probability and probability distributions, descriptive statistics, sampling distributions, estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and regression analysis. Our emphasis will be on developing statistical reasoning and intuition, understanding when and why particular methods are appropriate, and applying those methods to real-world problems. Rather than simply memorizing formulas, you will learn to select appropriate statistical methods, carry out analyses, interpret results, evaluate assumptions, and communicate conclusions in the context of the problem being studied.

title: STAT 312. Basic Statistics for Engineering and Science
text:
Important technical concepts
Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:

Build, use, and interpret graphical and numerical summaries of data.
Apply fundamental concepts of probability, including conditional probability, independence, random variables, and probability distributions, to engineering and scientific problems.
Identify and work with commonly used discrete and continuous probability distributions, and recognize situations in which they provide appropriate models.
Understand sampling variability and sampling distributions, including the role of the Central Limit Theorem in statistical inference.
Use sample data to estimate unknown population parameters and quantify uncertainty using standard errors and confidence intervals.
Formulate appropriate statistical hypotheses, conduct hypothesis tests, interpret p-values, and draw conclusions in the context of an engineering or scientific problem.
Build, interpret, and evaluate simple linear regression and correlation models, and use regression models for estimation and prediction.
Use appropriate statistical tools and software, when needed, to support statistical calculations, data analysis, and interpretation.
Interpret and communicate statistical results clearly using appropriate terminology, notation, reasoning, and evidence.

title: STAT 312. Basic Statistics for Engineering and Science
text:
Important statistical and problem-solving skills
The following skills are essential both within and beyond Statistics, and demonstrably improve your own learning:

Move beyond a “homework only” study approach. Develop a deeper understanding of the material through continued review, reflection, and practice.
Develop the ability to translate an engineering or scientific question into an appropriate statistical problem.
Think critically about data and determine which statistical method is appropriate and why.
Develop statistical intuition rather than relying solely on memorized formulas.
Think creatively and build confidence when applying course concepts in unfamiliar or open-ended settings.
Be comfortable working through challenges and mistakes, and use them as opportunities to refine your understanding.
Clearly explain and justify your approach, calculations, and conclusions.
Connect statistical concepts to real-world engineering and scientific applications.
Contribute to a welcoming, respectful, and engaged learning environment.

Md Mutasim Billah, PhD

Notes from “your instructor”



Greetings! You can call me Bill or Dr. Billah or Professor Billah & I use he/him pronouns. Back when I was an undergrad student, I didn’t have the best experience in Intro Stat - those courses often emphasized formulas over real understanding. That experience has shaped my teaching - I concentrate on illustrating how statistical theories connect and can be applied in the real world. I’m excited to teach STAT 312 and to create a more meaningful experience - one that helps all students feel confident applying it beyond the classroom. My methodological research lies at the intersection of statistical genetics, biostatistics, and genomics. My current research interests include developing novel statistical methods and computationally efficient bioinformatics tools, leveraging modern machine- and deep-learning approaches analyze high-dimensional next-generation sequencing and multi-omics data to identify genes and regulatory mechanisms underlying complex diseases. Outside of my academic work, I enjoy spending time outdoors with family and friends or cooking variety of foods. If you can’t find me anywhere, I might be busy playing soccer or exploring new worlds on my PS5 Pro!

Thriving in STAT 312






🗓️ Plan Ahead



You should plan to spend ~6-9 hours on any 3-credit course, including class time. Stay up-to-date on the course schedule and carve out time for studying & doing homework.








✅ Do the Things



At minimum, thriving in this course requires the completion of some concrete tasks. Complete all assignments, regularly attend & engage in class, complete practice problems (PP), and check the PP solutions.

If your main focus is on checking off some boxes, you won’t get much out of this course (or college in general). Deeper, enduring learning requires more. Carve out time to rewrite, reflect upon, & review your notes. Summarize concepts in your own words.








🎉 Engage, Ask Questions, Have Fun

title: Collecting and Summarizing Data
text:
Statistics is the science of collecting, analyzing, and interpreting data.


Engineers collect data from experiments, manufacturing processes, and systems.
Engineers analyze data to understand patterns and relationships.
Engineers interpret data to make decisions and improve processes.





A factory is manufacturing bolts that should be exactly 2 inches long.


Measuring the length of all bolts (a census) may be:

too time consuming,
too expensive,
or impossible.

Instead, we can collect a sample of bolts.





A random sample of 5 bolts yields the following measurements, in inches:
[ {2.003, 1.999, 2.006, 1.996, 2.001} ]

Population: The set of all people or things being studied, i.e., all possible observations.
Sample: The subset of the population from which information is actually collected.




Consider again the measurements:
[ {2.003, 1.999, 2.006, 1.996, 2.001} ]
The data have variability.


Identify the source(s) of the variation.
Reduce the variation.





The bolts are being produced by two different machines:


Machine A
Machine B


This gives us one possible source of variation in bolt length.



Each machine has three speed settings:


Slow: 500 bolts/minute
Medium: 1000 bolts/minute
Fast: 2000 bolts/minute


Now we have two possible sources of variation:


Machine
Production speed





There are several options.


Retrospective Study
Use data that have been collected in the past.
Observational Study
Observe the process in the present and collect data.
Designed Experiment
Exhibit maximum control over when, where, and how the data are collected.

title: R and RStudio Resources
text:
Crowd-sourced R functions
RStudio cheatsheets
Google it! If you have a question about R, someone else probably asked it. Add “R tidyverse” to your search term.
Example: scatterplot R tidyverse
Note about AI for code: AI tools can be useful for troubleshooting code, interpreting error messages, and improving your understanding of what a piece of code is doing. You may also use AI when provided course code unexpectedly stops working, for example, because an R package has been updated, a function has changed, or you encounter installation or compatibility issues. However, please avoid using AI as your first resort for writing R code or solving an assignment. Start with the lecture notes, class examples, provided code, and practice problems. AI tools may suggest unnecessarily complicated, unfamiliar, or even incorrect approaches that differ substantially from what we use in class. If you do use AI for coding assistance, make sure you understand every line of the resulting code and can explain what it does and why it works. AI should help you understand and troubleshoot your code, not replace your own statistical reasoning or problem-solving.
